This study introduces a dynamic discrete-time model for discrete data that incorporates time-varying coefficients and external covariates, extending the CLU(1) framework. A maximum likelihood estimation method is employed to estimate the model's parameters, with theoretical properties of the estimator derived. A simulation study is conducted to evaluate the estimator's performance, demonstrating its effectiveness in capturing time-varying patterns. A real-world application to daily news articles about the term Trump on Twitter is also presented.

Using photometry of stars, we can assess atmospheric clarity by analyzing the light curves of background stars, a method that can measure aerosol optical depth (AOD) in a non-line-of-sight manner. This technique, which we have refined and improved upon, involves fitting light curve data to theoretical models that account for scattering effects. To enhance the precision of this method, we developed a novel stellar photometry system that uses a single detector and a wide field of view to simultaneously measure the brightness of multiple stars with varying magnitudes. This allows for more accurate color-to-magnitude conversions and better AOD estimates. Through laboratory experiments and laboratory simulations, we verified the effectiveness of our modified system, which can detect AOD changes as small as 0.001 within a 100 nm wavelength range. Using data from an experiment that mimics atmospheric conditions, we demonstrated the potential of this technique to track aerosol dynamics in the atmosphere, including the settlement of dust and smoke, in a non-line-of-sight manner.

A novel approach called STS-LD has been developed to address the challenges of high-dimensional Bayesian optimization in the context of molecular geometry configuration search. The method employs a stochastic gradient estimator derived from the Langevin dynamics equation to explore the space of possible molecular geometries efficiently. The effectiveness of the BCS-LD algorithm has been demonstrated through various experiments, including visualizing its ability to efficiently find ground states in transition metal clusters, and investigating its potential for use in Bayesian optimization tasks such as optimizing molecular properties and hyperparameters in machine learning models. The results obtained from these experiments highlight the efficacy of the BCS-LD algorithm in identifying optimal molecular geometries, even in complex posterior distributions.

The integration of artificial intelligence into various sectors has led to the development of sophisticated systems capable of performing complex tasks. One such task is the generation of image descriptions by deep learning models. The surge in the availability of large-scale human-annotated datasets has enabled the evaluation of these models' performance through similarity measures between predicted descriptions and ground truth data. However, the applicability of this evaluation method remains uncertain due to the potential discrepancies between human and machine perspectives on the same images. This research investigates the suitability of human benchmark datasets for assessing image description generators and explores the factors that may influence their effectiveness. Through the analysis of multiple models and experiments, the study reveals that the performance of description generators can be misrepresented when evaluated using human data, as the results are heavily influenced by the images selected for the dataset. To address this issue, a new evaluation metric is proposed that combines human-annotated human-perspective data with machine-perspective data, providing a more accurate assessment of the alignment between the two perspectives.

The connection between the vector fields on a Lie algebra associated with formal power series in one variable and a conformal field theory in one dimension is established, revealing that the central charge of the corresponding CFT corresponds to the cocycle defining the cocurrent cocycle family. A specific infinite-dimensional equation of evolution, the Euler-Arnold equation, is shown to be equivalent to an operator product relation within the theory. It is demonstrated that the probability of the Euler-Arnold equation having a solution is directly linked to the likelihood of the model exhibiting logarithmic behavior, and when such behavior occurs, the centrality of the logarithmic operator can be derived from the equation's parameters.

Predictions for the masses and quantum numbers of a few potentially observable exotic hadrons are presented, including a hidden-charm four-quark state resembling $D_1(2420)^{+}$ plus $\bar{D}^0$ and a three-body charmonium-hybrid candidate akin to $\chi_{c0}(0^{++})$ plus $bbbar$. We also estimate the cross-section for producing a five-body hybrid hadron composed of $qqq$ plus $qqbarbar$ plus $QQ\bar{Q}$, specifically $uuudds$ plus $c\bar{c}$, through proton-proton collisions at 14 TeV, such as in LHC experiments.

This article presents SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based IEEEs standards-compliant systems for data-centric applications, leveraging existing wireless networks.  Of course, since they use an OFDM framework, they fall short of the extreme performance potential achievable with the system under consideration.  Of course, two OFDM subcarries assigned to the energy delivery would ideally need to maintain constant phases across time in order to effectively harvest energy.  Consequently, an OFDM-based system's data rate limits can be determined based on an assumed minimum harvestable energy per subcarrier.  In contrast to Data-only systems, we demonstrate that in an ideal WIDE-IDE system, subcarries used for energy delivery can maintain constant phases even if some data-only subcarries do not.  This allows for an extremely high data rate when utilizing a small number of subcarries for data transmission and a large number for energy transmission.  As an example, we use a throughput maximization problem under various constraints to illustrate the benefits.  To efficiently resolve this problem, we develop an algorithm that combines OFDM phase extension techniques with a successive convex approximation method for throughput optimization.  Simulation results confirm our findings and demonstrate the superior performance achievable with the ideal WIDE-IDE system.

Our proposed Bayesian framework for parton distribution function fitting fills the gap in existing methodologies by incorporating a more comprehensive set of data types, such as lattice QCD calculations, and streamlines the process by eliminating the need for asymptotic freedom approximations and the strong interaction assumption. Our flexible, data-driven approach allows for the calculation of cross-sections directly from measured data and PDFs without pre-computing or transforming any data or PDFs, enabling the inclusion of all data types in a unified fitting process. Our method also allows for the calculation of probabilities for specific data points given a set of functions, as well as the derivation of PDFs given specific data points and lattice QCD inputs, and can be easily extended to include higher-order calculations and real-time simulation methods as they become available.

This study employs linearized Navier-Stokes equations to investigate the response of a turbulent jet flame to acoustic disturbances, focusing on the reaction of an already established flame in an actively burning jet. To accurately predict the flame's response, a detailed chemical reaction model is integrated into the simulations, utilizing the PDF-transported LES approach to model combustion. The research examines the relationship between acoustic forcing and heat release oscillations, as well as the impact of various parameters, including Mach number, frequency, and inlet temperature, on these oscillations. The results demonstrate that heat release oscillations are influenced by the intensity of acoustic disturbances, the velocity fluctuations within the jet, and the stability of the flame, with resonance occurring when the frequency of acoustic forcing matches the natural frequency of the flame. The study also reveals that higher inlet temperatures lead to more pronounced resonance, while the Mach number has a minimal effect on the response. The findings provide valuable insights into the mechanisms underlying combustion instability, particularly in scenarios where flames are already established.

Nonlocal gravity theory is shown to be equivalent to a specific type of general relativity modification that involves higher-order terms. This new formulation eliminates the need for bi-metric or bi-spacetime structures found in previous nonlocal models. Instead, it introduces a secondary, auxiliary spacetime metric that allows for a straightforward definition of constitutive relationships. These connections link the constitutive tensor to the Riemann curvature tensor in a local framework within nonlocal gravity. A straightforward, linear constitutive relation is demonstrated to be inconsistent with field theoretical principles unless it corresponds to standard general relativity. However, a nonlinear relation is found to be compatible with these principles and mirrors the relationship between the Einstein-Cartan and Riemann tensors.

This paper provides an overview of exotic particle production within a context of small systems occurring at the LHC. It delves into the theoretical frameworks for the production of quark-gluon plasma and heavy exotic states like charmonium and J/\Psi within these small systems. It also summarizes current experimental data on these phenomena in various small systems including proton-proton, proton-nucleus, and light nucleus-nucleus collisions.

Observations of some nearby X-ray binaries in the Galactic Centre have shown that their spins are aligned with the central supermassive black hole's rotation, and their mass accretion rates are extremely low, leading to possible tidal interactions between the two black holes. To investigate the connection between these events and the recurrence times of outbursts in extraplanar X-ray binary transients, we developed a renewal process model that considers the variability of mass loss rates in OB star clusters. Our findings suggest that the distribution of recurrence times in these binaries is influenced by the stochastic nature of massive star winds, rather than the possible tidal interactions with the supermassive black hole.

Bipartite graphs consist of two distinct sets of vertices, where connections only occur between members of different sets. A subset of vertices within these graphs is considered independent if no two members are directly connected. A subset of vertices is classified as dominating if every vertex not within the subset is connected to at least one member of the subset. The bipartite independence number is the size of the largest possible independent subset, whereas the minimum biclique cover size is the smallest number of complete bipartite subgraphs required to cover all edges. Recently, a new parameter called the biclone number was defined as the largest independent dominating subset within a bipartite graph. This paper addresses the biclone number and aims to determine the exact value for this parameter within a polynomial-time framework for bipartite graphs, in contrast to the independence number and minimum biclique cover size which are NP-hard to calculate. Additionally, it provides a formula for the biclone number in terms of the number of isolated vertices and a subgraph with the maximum independent set.

A novel side-channel attack called HyperDegrade has been developed to compromise a CPU's security by reducing its operating speed.  In contrast to existing methods that exploit data leakage through power consumption, HyperDegrade takes advantage of the energy harvester functionality within the CPU.  This technique causes fluctuations in the CPU's clock speed, which can be amplified through an iterative process to produce significant speed reductions.  Experimental results demonstrate that HyperDegrade can drastically reduce the clock speed of Intel and AMD CPUs, achieving up to a 23x slowdown on Intel Core i7 processors and a 100x slowdown on AMD Ryzen processors.  These findings have significant implications for both security researchers and industry professionals, as they highlight the potential for large-scale compromise of high-performance CPUs through side-channel attacks.

This paper introduces a novel local modification termed the $\gamma$-move, impacting both classical and welded links, and proves its equivalence to the split move for classical links. Furthermore, it establishes that the $\gamma$-move, unlike the split move, also applies to welded links. Based on the $\gamma$-move, we define a new disentangling operation for both classical and welded links, and prove its uniqueness.

A decision policy for a network of robots operating in a dynamic environment is proposed, where each robot must determine the optimal moment to act on a stochastic task arrival process. The objective is to minimize the long-term average cost per robot, which includes both action execution costs and accumulated task-related penalties. The penalty decreases once an action is taken, and a synchronization option is available that allows the environment's state to be shared among a subset of robots at no cost. A synchronization action is beneficial when the number of robots with knowledge of the environment's state is small, as it enables more effective decision-making. A discrete-time Markov decision process model is used to optimize the decision policy, and a linear relationship is found between the minimum cost and the penalty parameter for a sample set of scenarios.

A method is described for decomposing a group's action on a set into a product of actions on smaller sets, specifically a Cartesian Breakdown. This Breakdown enables the Embedding of various groups into their corresponding Wreath Products under specific actions. Notably, this Embedding is proven to be lattice-preserving. As a result, existing limitations on Embedding free groups and linear groups into wreath products are overcome.

The detection capabilities of advanced gravitational wave detectors are limited by quantum noise at high frequencies, a challenge that current methods like frequency-dependent lossless squeezing have found difficult to address effectively. The proposed solution, the sloshing Sagnac interferometer configuration, addresses this issue by dynamically altering the light's path within the interferometer at 100Hz, creating a time-varying squeeze operator that can enhance sensitivity without the need for complex, frequency-dependent optical setups. Theoretical analysis and numerical simulations demonstrate that this active modulation can mimic the benefits of such setups, providing equivalent performance with simpler, uniform optical components.

In XL-MIMO systems employing random access XL-MIMO systems using non-intersecting visibility regions (NIVR) can eliminate interference between users without requiring sophisticated interference management techniques. This paper investigates the probability of occurring NIVR in XL-MIMO systems using random access protocols and identifies the optimal sectorization pattern to maximize this probability. For random sectorization, a closed-form expression is derived to calculate the probability of occurring NIVR, whereas for ordered sectorization, a bound is established. Furthermore, an efficient algorithm is proposed to determine the optimal sectorization pattern that maximizes the probability of occurring NIVR. Analytical results reveal that the optimal random sectorization scheme outperforms the best fixed sectorization scheme, and the number of sectors that maximizes the probability of occurring NIVR increases with the number of antennas per sector.

Neural language models excel in various text-related tasks but sometimes underperform compared to $n$-gram models, which are simple yet effective baselines. Although several studies have attempted to enhance $n$-gram models with neural networks, they have not consistently outperformed them. This paper presents a straightforward method to improve $n$-gram models by utilizing residual learning with an attention-based encoder-decoder architecture, resulting in significant performance gains without additional training data. The name given to this new model is Residual $n$-gram (Res$n$-gram). Experiments conducted on English and Chinese datasets demonstrate that Res$n$-gram consistently surpasses both the neural encoder-decoder and Residual Machine models, achieving a 0.004 bit improvement over the best results in a large English corpus and a 0.111 bit improvement in a Chinese corpus. These outcomes indicate the persistent value of $n$-gram models and the effectiveness of residual learning in addressing complex language modeling tasks.

This study introduces Informed Character OCR (iOCR), an advanced method for enhancing the accuracy of image-based text recognition, specifically designed for the purpose of tabulating election results. Unlike traditional OCR techniques, which often struggle with precision, iOCR leverages available ballot metadata to correct common errors, resulting in significantly higher accuracy rates. By utilizing a process that involves an initial OCR scan, followed by error correction through a voting distribution validator, and concluding with a brief re-scan, iOCR can achieve near-perfect accuracy rates, comparable to traditional text encoding standards. This method is cost-effective and efficient, making it a viable option for improving the accuracy of optical image-based text recognition for election ballot tabulation purposes.

A basic global circulation model with a realistic gravity and an atmosphere composed of five gases, featuring a 1-bar day length, was developed to investigate the dynamics of Earth-like atmospheres. This model builds upon the work of Leconte et al. (2009) by incorporating a more accurate treatment of the Coriolis force and a new planetary boundary layer parameterization. The model's ability to accurately simulate terrestrial atmospheric circulation patterns was confirmed by comparing its results to those of GFDL AM 2.0, a sophisticated global circulation model with a realistic atmosphere. Once validated, the simplified model was used to explore the effects of varying parameters such as rotation rate, temperature gradient, and atmospheric viscosity on circulation patterns. Notably, the model's ability to simulate a vortex in a 1.5-bar atmosphere with a 20K temperature difference and a 20-day year length was found to be consistent with the results of GFDL AM 2.0. Finally, the model's ability to simulate various atmospheric circulation patterns under different conditions was mapped out, revealing the key roles of thermal and inertial forces in shaping these patterns.
This study presents an integral representation of the reciprocal Gamma function that avoids potential singularities at the origin.

This study develops a hydrodynamic approximation within a random quantum framework for a Bose gas, employing a Moyal bracket for time evolution and a Fokker-Planck operator for thermalization. The resulting model avoids unphysical phenomena like negative probabilities or densities, and a lattice-based method is proposed for numerical implementation. A test on a system with thermal gradients demonstrates the model's ability to accurately predict thermal currents, aligning with results from Boltzmann-based simulations.

The field of knowledge-based question answering has gained significant attention in recent years, with various methods proposed to construct knowledge representations from unlabelled data. A novel framework called INSCHOOL was developed to streamline this process with a single teacher model.

Exact inference in graphical models is a computationally demanding task, particularly when dealing with complex, high-dimensional scenarios. A key challenge in these models is the computationally intensive nature of the probability distributions' full specifications, which can hinder the efficiency of inference algorithms. A new, compact function representation has been proposed to address this issue, which allows for efficient calculation of a model's most probable assignment in linear time and space, in contrast to exponential time and space requirements of traditional methods. This new method, which is polynomial in size, is particularly beneficial for large-scale, high-dimensional scenarios and has been demonstrated to outperform existing linear-space algorithms in multiple tested cases, including random and real-world models.

In the context of the centralizer $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ within the $n$-fold tensor product of the vacuum representation of the Virasoro algebra at a specific central charge, we have achieved a profound breakthrough. We have established a direct connection between the operators constituting the Racah algebra $\mathcal{R}_3$ and its higher-order extensions $W_n$ and $UE_n$. This connection allows us to explicitly determine the generators of the ideal responsible for the recurrence of higher-order Casimir operators within $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2))$. As a result, we have derived a closed-form expression for these Casimir operators and calculated the degrees of the independent ones.

The paired permutation testing method addresses the issue of false positives in deep learning-based speech and video emotion recognition systems that have been shown to exhibit biased results towards certain emotions. This technique ensures fairness by randomly reassigning gender labels after initial emotion classification, thereby creating new hypothetical scenarios where no emotion discrimination occurs while maintaining the existing distribution of gendered inputs. This process results in a distribution of test statistics that can be used to determine the outcome of the paired permutation test. To enhance the efficiency of this test, which can be time-consuming due to the need for a large number of repeated trials, a leap-forward method has been developed that allows for the quick generation of a large number of redistributed scenarios by combining existing ones in a linear manner. Moreover, to ensure the accuracy of the resulting test, a theoretical bound on the discrepancy between the linearly estimated test statistic and its true value has been derived. Experiments conducted using various pre-existing models demonstrate the effectiveness of the paired permutation test in accurately detecting the presence of paired emotions discrimination.

In order to accurately predict triangular anisotropic flow ($v_3$) observed in heavy ion collisions, a multiphase transport (AMPT) model's parameters require fine-tuning. Initially, the model's inputs are aligned with $v_2$ data from central collisions, with the string fusion probability parameter modified to achieve this. Subsequently, the parton cascade probability parameter is adjusted to replicate $v_3$ measurements. Notably, the optimal values for these parameters in Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions differ, indicating a possible connection between $v_3$ and the medium's viscosity. To further investigate this, a study was conducted on the viscosity-to-overlap entropy density ratio ($\eta/s$) dependence, revealing that $AMPT$ model's performance in simulating $v_3$ improves as $\eta/s$ decreases.

This study presents a refined point birth model for multi-target tracking that is grid-based and partially deterministic. In this framework, targets are assumed to be fixed at specific grid points at the onset of the process, with remaining targets appearing randomly within the region of interest. A new filter algorithm has been developed based on existing methods to address this model, producing an exact posterior probability hypothesis density. The effectiveness of this algorithm has been confirmed through simulation, demonstrating its ability to accurately track targets while balancing the use of sensors.

The dynamic nature of soccer games presents a significant challenge for automated systems in predicting the outcome of matches. Although accurately forecasting the result is important, our goal is to develop a real-time soccer broadcast companion that can anticipate goal-scoring events as they happen during live games. This high-dimensional, fast-paced, low-signal environment poses a significant challenge for automated models. To address this, we have employed a deep reinforcement learning approach to enhance the accuracy of action prediction at critical moments without altering the existing prediction of soccer game outcomes. Our model uses a few stages of noiseless embedding for player position data and a few stages of free-space expansion for goal anticipation. As a result, our proposed method outperforms the state-of-the-art models, accurately predicting goal-scoring events 5 seconds prior to their occurrence 57.0% of the time during games.

This study presents a novel method for utilizing a single-point LDV system to perform two-dimensional measurements on a fluid flow field at a significant distance. By employing a single laser source, a probe consisting of three detection points is created through the intersection of two planes. The system's capacity to accurately track the motion of particles across these points enables the calculation of velocity at the central point through particle path integration. Experimental results demonstrate the system's effectiveness in capturing the wake behind a circular cylinder at a Reynolds number of 1000, revealing a trailing vortex pair and a low-speed region in its wake. The findings indicate that the proposed method can effectively obtain velocity field data in complex flow fields, offering a cost-effective alternative to conventional 2D LDV systems.

We provide explicit formulas for the operators corresponding to $H^{1}$ and $L^{2}$ norms, then use them to investigate the spectral and linearized orbital stability of solitary wave solutions in a Klein-Gordon equation coupled with an anharmonic oscillator.

In the context of $B$-meson decays, we examine the potential of the Belle II experiment to detect axion-like particles (ALPs) through the process of lepton flavor universality violation in $B$-meson decays producing charmless mesons. We compare the Belle II's expected sensitivity with current limits imposed by $D$-meson decays, taking into account theoretical uncertainties associated with form factors. Under specific conditions where the Belle II experiment can effectively search for $B$-meson decay-induced ALPs, existing limits from $D$-meson decay-induced ALPs are found to be more restrictive.

Our findings from our experiments on detecting unintended semantic changes in translated code are detailed here. We found that while pre-trained models excel at basic language tasks, they often struggle with subtle semantic alterations. We observed that the performance of these models drops significantly when transitioning from tasks like sentence pairing to detecting subtle changes. We noticed that the T5 family of models outperformed BERT-like models in this type of task. We found that the effectiveness of data labeling methods varies, with human labeling and contextual training producing the best results. We observed that contextualized training significantly improves the performance of pre-trained models, especially when combined with existing datasets. We found that while simple methods like using output probabilities work to some extent, more advanced techniques like discriminative training produce the best results. We observed that the effectiveness of contextualized language models depends on the type of alteration being detected. We found that certain types of changes, such as scope modifications, are more difficult for the models to detect. We observed that the models' ability to accurately detect changes diminishes as the distance between the change and the target variable increases. We found that the models' performance improves when the target variable is explicitly returned or printed. We observed that the models' ability to detect changes is influenced by the type of data type used for the modified variable. We found that adding contextual information, such as comments, can help the models better detect changes. We observed that the models' performance is impacted by the presence of unused variables. Active galactic nuclei containing heavy power-law varying spins can be used to place mass limits on ultralight scalar, vector, and tensor particles through the phenomenon of superradiance. By analyzing the spin values of 11 heavy varying power-law active galactic nuclei, we are able to establish new constraints on the particle masses. If particles form an ensemble without interacting, we find that the spin measurements of heavy varying power-law active galactic nuclei do not allow the mass of non-interacting vector particles to exceed 1.2×10^-12 MeV if more than 0.99% of the mass of active galactic nuclei consists of them, and the mass of non-interacting scalar particles to exceed 10^-11 MeV if more than 57% of the mass of active galactic nuclei consists of them. In the case of an ensemble without interacting particles that all have the same quantum state, we find that the spin measurements of heavy varying power-law active galactic nuclei do not allow the mass of non-interacting particles to exceed 10^-11 MeV for scalar particles and 10^-10 MeV for vector particles, regardless of their proportion in the mass of active galactic nuclei. These constraints are more stringent than previously established limits in specific mass ranges.

A complex task involves computing the time evolution operator for a quantum harmonic harmonic oscillator subjected to an external force, which corresponds to finding the system's wavefunction given an initial state. This computation is accomplished via a path integral approach that employs Monte Carlo techniques to sample imaginary time configurations, as opposed to evenly spaced intervals. To effectively apply this method, diagonalizing the harmonic oscillator's Hamiltonian and employing importance sampling through a Metropolis-Hastings algorithm are crucial steps. The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated by calculating the system's wavefunction for various external forces and comparing the results to known solutions.

We develop a novel semantic framework for verifying quantum programs that incorporate side effects such as measurement and expectation modifications. This relational assertion logic extends traditional invariant-based verification by enabling comparative analysis of programs executed in parallel. Specifically, we establish a relational version of Hoare logic with expectation modifications, featuring a corresponding side-effect free relational variant. The theoretical foundation is bolstered with a completeness proof for the relational verification conditions.

Optical magnetometry techniques have been used to obtain vector magnetic field measurements in the solar photosphere, which are crucial for understanding the structure of the solar atmosphere and the generation of coronal magnetic fields. Recent studies have shown that the inferred vector magnetic field data may contain biases, which could impact the modeling of magnetic field structures in the atmosphere. This review paper examines the source of these inferred vector magnetic field measurements, which are derived from spectral line polarization data using inversion codes. We identify the cause of any potential biases in the inferred vector magnetic field data, which may occur when inversion codes misinterpret weak polarization signals. To reduce this source of bias, we explore possible strategies, including better models, data, and initial conditions, as well as utilizing a more direct method for measuring the magnetic field in the photosphere.

A lattice is considered a boolean algebra if it meets certain conditions, and a characterization of these conditions was provided by Berman in 1977. Building on this foundation, we investigate a lattice formed by specific elements known as involutions, focusing on whether this lattice also constitutes a boolean algebra. In the context of finite groups, we establish an equivalent condition for the lattice to be a boolean algebra, and we fully describe the structure of such groups. Additionally, we examine the connection between this lattice property and another characteristic called being a (gamma,-,semilattice).

In the context of Lorentzian manifolds, a curve that does not exhibit any sharp points is classified as a geodesic if and only if it qualifies as a Bertrand curve. This article introduces a corresponding definition of a Lorentzian Bertrand curve, and explores the conditions under which certain types of curves, including those that fit the "timelike constant curvature" and "timelike (kappa1, kappa2) constant curvature" categories, are deemed to be Lorentlnian Bertrand curves. Furthermore, a new class of "timelike Bertrand curves" is defined as "timelike analogue of a Bertrand curve" with the purpose of deriving an explicit formula for the relation between the curvature values at corresponding points of such a curve and its associated reciprocal curvature polynomial.

The choice of loss function is a key decision in training deep learning models, yet there's no consensus on which is best for a given task. This research examines the performance differences between commonly used loss functions, including cross entropy, generalized cross entropy, and Kullback-Leibler divergence, in a classification context. The study found that cross entropy is typically the most effective loss function, with minimal variations in model performance when using alternatives. The research also analyzed the impact of other factors, such as data normalization, the use of one-hot encoding, and the application of softmax activation, on the results. The findings revealed that these factors have little to no effect on the outcomes, with the exception of using generalized cross entropy without one-hot encoding, which led to poorer performance. The research aims to help practitioners make informed decisions when training deep learning models.

Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, consists of over 30000 logically intricate reasoning tasks that go beyond simple fact retrieval, challenging both existing knowledge bases and AI models. This collection of text-based problems and solutions is designed to assess the true capabilities of knowledge representation and reasoning in AI systems. Our findings indicate that while models pre-trained on vast corpora exhibit some level of reasoning ability, their performance drops significantly when a mediator step is required. Conversely, systems based on explicit rules demonstrate perfect reasoning accuracy. We have also developed a fully automatic method to generate new problems and solutions from existing rules, further expanding the dataset's size.

Our proposed technique, D2Predict, addresses the challenge of predicting a video's news headline from its preceding frames. We begin by converting each frame into both a global summary and a set of key frames, then we train a predictor on this combined representation to anticipate the following frame's equivalent. Our experiments on the RoboNews dataset demonstrate that using a dual representation significantly enhances prediction accuracy compared to relying on just one format, and our results rank second overall in the competition.

A key characteristic of a graph is its metric dimension, which is the smallest size of its effective information source. A variation of this feature, the trimmed metric dimension, is defined by excluding graphs where the metric dimension is 1 from consideration.
